ds: Improper payments or favours linked to public or private procurement, including kickbacks to buyers, inflated contract prices, bid rigging and phantom suppliers. Banks and corporates can detect patterns in supplier payments, related parties and post-award flows.

src.t: OECD, Recommendation of the Council on Public Procurement (2015)
OECD, Preventing Corruption in Public Procurement (2016)
OECD, Guidelines for Fighting Bid Rigging in Public Procurement (2009)
FATF, Laundering the Proceeds of Corruption (2011)

rat: Supplier payments and post-award flows to connected parties in procurement.

ind.n: Contract price well above market or estimate
ind.cx: Awarded price materially exceeds engineers' estimates or comparable contracts without justification.
ind.fp: Complexity, scope change and inflation can legitimately inflate prices.
ind.ds: Price paid differs sharply from market value, comparable sales or estimates without commercial justification.
ind.cn: Transaction price materially different from market value

ind.n: Repeated wins by the same supplier with narrow margins
ind.cx: One supplier repeatedly wins just below competitors or in rotation among a small group.
ind.fp: Niche markets may have few capable bidders.
ind.ds: One supplier repeatedly wins just below competitors or in rotation among a small group.

ind.n: Post-award payments from supplier to buyer-linked accounts
ind.cx: Winning supplier transfers funds to persons or companies connected to the procuring official shortly after payment.
ind.fp: Supplier subcontracting may pay related parties innocently.
ind.ds: Winning supplier transfers funds to persons or companies connected to the procuring official shortly after payment.

ind.n: Supplier lacks capacity for awarded contract
ind.cx: Awardee has no relevant staff, assets or experience and subcontracts nearly all work.
ind.fp: Project vehicles are often newly formed and sub-contract widely.
ind.ds: Awardee has no relevant staff, assets or experience and subcontracts nearly all work.

ind.n: Frequent contract variations or change orders
ind.cx: Scope and price rise significantly through repeated amendments shortly after award.
ind.fp: Genuine scope changes are common in construction and IT.
ind.ds: Scope and price rise significantly through repeated amendments shortly after award.

ind.n: Emergency or single-source award with weak justification
ind.cx: Use of urgency or sole-source exceptions for non-urgent purchases.
ind.fp: Real emergencies exist and justify fast awards.
ind.ds: Use of urgency or sole-source exceptions for non-urgent purchases.

ind.n: Phantom or fictitious supplier on vendor master
ind.cx: Vendor with no verifiable address, tax number or deliveries shares details with an employee or another vendor.
ind.fp: Data entry errors can create apparent duplicates.
ind.ds: Vendor has no verifiable address, tax number or deliveries, or shares address or bank details with an employee.
ind.cn: Vendor linked to employee or without verifiable existence

ind.n: Rapid bank account changes or payments to unrelated accounts for suppliers
ind.cx: Supplier asks to redirect payments to accounts held by third parties, often after award.
ind.fp: Suppliers legitimately change banks or factor receivables.
ind.ds: Payment is requested to, or credited to, a personal, third-party or differently named account rather than the contracted payee.
ind.cn: Payment directed to personal or third-party account

ctl.ds: Compares declared unit prices, award values, fees and ancillary costs with reference databases, estimates and comparable contracts, and requires documented rationale for outliers. It detects over- and under-invoicing and inflated awards.

Tests bidding and award data for rotation, cover bids, price clustering, splitting, variations and exceptions to competition, and requires independent cost and justification review. It detects collusion and corrupt awards.
Participates in sector, regulator and public-private forums and platform cooperation to receive and share typologies and indicators where lawful. It keeps scenarios current.
Links accounts, devices, addresses, directors and beneficiaries to surface rings, shared attributes and flow structures that single-account views miss. It supports detection of organised networks.

ctl.n: Public-funds payment monitoring and contract evidence
ctl.ds: Flags credits from public bodies to personal or new accounts, atypical state-to-private flows and onward movement, and requires contracts and tender evidence for payments from state entities. It targets diversion of public money.

Obliges counterparties to disclose and obtain approval for subcontractors, together with beneficial ownership details. It prevents work or funds being passed to undisclosed parties who would not pass due diligence.

Tests whether an entity has real operations such as premises, staff, stock and contracts through documents, site or virtual visits, open-source footprint and shell-risk indicators. It helps identify shell and front companies with no genuine activity.
Clusters customers, vendors and entities that share addresses, phones, devices, officers or bank details, including against staff records. It reveals common control and hidden relationships.

Verifies new vendors and suppliers before first payment through registry checks, site or call validation and review against the existing vendor base. It prevents fictitious or controlled vendors being set up to extract funds.
Verifies instructions, detail changes and unusual requests by contacting the customer on a channel held on file, never one supplied in the request. It defeats impersonation and account takeover.

Checks the payee name against the destination account before release and warns on no-match or close-match, and flags payee-name mismatches against contracted entities. It interrupts misdirected, spoofed and fraudulent payments.
